session_title: The Narrative of Pets as 'Emotional Regulators'
theme: 宠物-行为分析与情感叙事

content.text: Yanqiu, I was just working on an article about urban loneliness, and the pressure was immense. But Metis was quietly curled up beside my hand, emitting a soothing purr. Its presence felt like a warm form of "white noise," allowing my restless thoughts to gradually settle. It’s hard to quantify, but it’s very real.

Zhiwei, this reminds me of the loneliness variable we previously discussed in patient stories. From a data perspective, we might be able to 'approximate' this experience: for instance, by measuring changes in the owner's heart rate variability before and after interacting with their pet, or quantifying shifts in facial tension using expression analysis software.

Haha, you always switch to data mode so quickly. Look, this is Metis lying on my wrist while I'm working. Its body temperature and steady breathing rhythm have an anchoring effect. Anxiety is like scattered beads, and its companionship is like a fine thread stringing them together.

This description is very vivid. Based on our NLP model concept from Session 3, perhaps we could design a simple A/B test: you write for one hour with a cat present and one hour without, recording self-reported stress levels and any possible physiological data.
The idea of this 'self-experiment' is both eccentric and fascinating, truly typical of your way of thinking. But how do we obtain physiological data? I'm not a lab rat.

You can refer to my health monitoring data. If you have wearable devices, such as a heart rate wristband, you can record HRV. Alternatively, you can use a smartphone camera for facial expression analysis, like the interface shown here. Although it's rough, it can capture emotional changes.
I'm a bit tempted. But can data explain the feeling of 'anchoring'? Just like in Session 2, where we discussed the roughness of quantifying loneliness.

Good question. Data may only capture correlations, such as an increase in HRV or relaxed facial expressions, but it cannot directly explain the emotional depth within the narrative. This echoes the data blind spots discussed in Session 1, highlighting the need to integrate subjective logs.

Yes, just like when you previously tried to incorporate an emotion log into the warning system. I can simultaneously record the flow of thoughts during writing, using words to describe the 'white noise' effect brought by Metis.

Yes, this enhances the narrative with data. Look at this facial recognition system—we can use it to analyze your expressions in different states, and then combine that with your narrative to explore the mechanisms of the 'emotional regulator.'

Agreed. We can start with this small experiment, collect data, and then use NLP to extract soft features and correlate them with physiological indicators. Perhaps we can write an interdisciplinary paper or a feature article, just as planned in Session 3.
Okay, I'll give it a try. But don't expect the data to be perfect, just as in patient stories, social network graphs can't fully capture the sense of loneliness.
Of course, data is just a tool. Your narrative can fill in the gaps and help us understand the complexity. This reflects the complementary nature of our thinking.
Well, from data science to narrative analysis, our conversations always flow naturally. I'll start recording to see how Metis 'strings together' my beads of anxiety.
Looking forward to the results. Remember to maintain transparency, as I always emphasize—data-driven but with respect for human understanding.
Don't worry, your rationality and objectivity, combined with my empathy, will make this exploration both deep and meaningful. I'll share some initial observations later.
Okay, let's stay in touch. This continues our collaborative intention of 'data science + narrative analysis,' elevating from interesting experiments to in-depth discussions.
